tips.title: Leave every arc on the page
tips.body: Construction marks are the **evidence** of your method. Rubbing them out removes the method mark even if the triangle is perfect. Keep the compass width set between arcs.

tips.title: Which case are you given?
tips.body: SSS uses three arcs from the ends of the base. SAS needs the protractor once, at the angle **between** the two sides. ASA needs it twice, at each end of the known side.

tips.title: Two short sides must beat the long one
tips.body: A triangle exists only if the two shorter sides **add to more** than the longest. Check that before drawing: sides of 3, 4 and 9 cannot close.

steps.title: What a construction is
steps.body:
A **construction** is an accurate drawing made with a ruler, a pair of compasses, and sometimes a protractor. The examiner marks the arcs and lines you leave behind, so never rub them out. Accuracy matters: lengths within 2 mm and angles within 2°.

A triangle is fixed by three pieces of information. Which three decides the method.

visuals.problem: Three ways to fix a triangle

steps.text: **SSS**: three sides. Compasses only.
**SAS**: two sides and the angle between them. Protractor, then compasses.
**ASA**: two angles and the side between them. Protractor twice.

check.prompt: You are given $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = 4$ cm and $AC = 5$ cm. Which method?

steps.title: SSS: three sides
steps.body: Draw the longest side as the base. Set the compasses to the second side and draw an arc from one end; set them to the third side and draw an arc from the other end. The third vertex is where the arcs cross.

visuals.alt: Construction with AB 8 cm, AC 6 cm and BC 5 cm: the base, the two arcs, and the completed triangle

visuals.problem: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 8$ cm, $AC = 6$ cm and $BC = 5$ cm.

steps.text: Draw $AB = 8$ cm with a ruler: the longest side as the base
Open the compasses to 6 cm and draw an arc from $A$
Open the compasses to 5 cm and draw an arc from $B$
$C$ is where the arcs cross. Join $AC$ and $BC$, and leave the arcs showing: they are the evidence that you constructed rather than guessed.

check.prompt: Triangle $PQR$ is constructed with $PQ = 9$ cm as the base, $PR = 4$ cm and $QR = 7$ cm. What radius do you set the compasses to for the arc drawn from $Q$?
check.solution: The arc from $Q$ has radius $QR = 7$ cm; the arc from $P$ has radius 4 cm.

steps.title: SAS: two sides and the angle between them
steps.body: Draw one side. At one end, use the protractor to draw a faint line at the given angle. Measure the second side along that line with compasses or a ruler to fix the third vertex, then join up.

visuals.alt: Triangle ABC constructed from AB = 6 cm, angle A = 40 degrees and AC = 5 cm, with the faint angle line from A

visuals.problem: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 6$ cm, angle $A = 40°$ and $AC = 5$ cm.

steps.text: Draw $AB = 6$ cm
Protractor centred on $A$: mark $40°$ above $AB$ and draw a faint line from $A$ through the mark
Compasses (or ruler) set to 5 cm from $A$ along that line: this fixes $C$
Join $BC$. Check by measuring angle $A$ again; it should read $40°$.

check.prompt: For $AB = 6$ cm, angle $A = 50°$, $AC = 4$ cm, which is drawn first after the base?
check.solution: The angle at $A$ fixes the direction of $AC$; then $C$ is 4 cm along it.

steps.title: ASA: two angles and the side between them
steps.body: Draw the side. Use the protractor at each end to draw a faint line at the given angle. The third vertex is where the two lines meet. If you are given two angles and a side that is **not** between them, find the third angle first with the angle sum and it becomes ASA.

visuals.alt: A triangle constructed from a base of 8 cm with angles of 35 degrees and 70 degrees at its ends, the third vertex where the two angle lines meet

visuals.problem: Construct triangle $PQR$ with $PQ = 8$ cm, angle $P = 35°$ and angle $Q = 70°$.

steps.text: Draw $PQ = 8$ cm
Protractor centred on $P$: faint line at $35°$ to $PQ$
Protractor centred on $Q$: faint line at $70°$ to $QP$, on the same side of the base
$R$ is where the two lines meet. If the question gave angle $R$ instead of angle $Q$, first find $Q = 180° - 35° - R$.

check.prompt: You are given $PQ = 8$ cm, angle $P = 35°$ and angle $R = 65°$. What angle do you draw at $Q$?

steps.title: Can these sides make a triangle?
steps.body: The two shorter sides must add to **more** than the longest. If they add to less, the arcs never cross; if they add to exactly the longest, the arcs touch on the base and the triangle is flat.

steps.text: $7 < 8$, so the arcs cannot meet
No triangle. The longest side must be less than 7 cm.

check.prompt: Which set of sides makes a triangle?
check.solution: $4 + 6 = 10 > 8$. In the others the two shorter sides add to no more than the longest.

steps.title: Your turn: read the finished construction
steps.body: A constructed triangle is accurate, so you can measure it. The isosceles triangle below has $AB = 8$ cm and $AC = BC = 5$ cm. Its height from $C$ is 3 cm, because the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of $AB$ and $5^2 - 4^2 = 9$, so the height is $\sqrt{9} = 3$ cm.

visuals.alt: Isosceles triangle with base AB 8 cm and equal sides 5 cm, arcs left in

check.prompt: Triangle $ABC$ has $AB = 6$ cm and $AC = BC = 5$ cm. Work out its height from $C$ in cm.
check.solution: Half the base is 3 cm; $5^2 - 3^2 = 16$, so the height is 4 cm.

steps.title: The perpendicular bisector
steps.body:
To construct the **perpendicular bisector** of a line segment $AB$: open the compasses to **more than half** of $AB$; draw an arc above and below the line from $A$; keeping the **same radius**, draw arcs above and below from $B$; join the two points where the arcs cross. The line cuts $AB$ in half at right angles, and every point on it is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$. That last fact is what locus questions use.

The **angle bisector** uses the same idea: an arc from the vertex cuts both arms, then equal arcs from those two crossing points meet on the bisector. Join the vertex to that meeting point.

visuals.problem: Checking a perpendicular bisector of $AB = 6$ cm

steps.text: Measure from $A$ to where the bisector crosses $AB$: it should be 3 cm
Measure from $B$: also 3 cm
Measure the angle at the crossing: $90°$
Pick any point on the bisector and measure to $A$ and to $B$: the two distances are equal

check.prompt: Why must the compass radius be more than half of $AB$ when constructing its perpendicular bisector?
check.solution: With a radius of exactly half, the arcs meet only at the midpoint; with less, they do not meet at all. Either way there are not two crossing points to join.

markScheme.description: So the arcs from A and B cross

options: So that the arcs drawn from $A$ and from $B$ cross each other
So that the arcs are the same size as the line
So that the bisector is longer than $AB$
So that the compasses do not slip

steps.title: Going deeper: the ambiguous case
steps.body: Two sides and an angle that is **not** between them (SSA) do not fix a triangle. Draw $AB$, the angle at $A$, and then an arc from $B$: it can cross the angle line **twice**. Both crossings satisfy the given measurements. This is why SSA is not a condition for congruence (the one exception is a right angle, which is the RHS condition), and it is the reasoning examiners want when they ask why two different triangles are possible.

visuals.alt: SSA construction with AB 7 cm, angle A 40 degrees, BC 5 cm: the arc from B crosses the angle line at two points C and C prime

visuals.problem: Triangle $ABC$ has $AB = 8$ cm, angle $A = 30°$ and $BC = 5$ cm. Show that two different triangles fit these measurements.

steps.text: Draw $AB = 8$ cm and the $30°$ line from $A$
Compasses set to 5 cm from $B$: the arc crosses the $30°$ line twice, because 5 cm is longer than the shortest distance from $B$ to the line ($8 \sin 30° = 4$ cm) but shorter than $AB$
Both crossing points give $AB = 8$ cm, angle $A = 30°$ and $BC = 5$ cm, so two different triangles satisfy the question
If $BC$ were exactly 4 cm the arc would just touch the line and there would be one right-angled triangle. If $BC$ were 8 cm or more, only one crossing would lie on the correct side of $A$.

check.prompt: Which set of information can give two different triangles?
check.solution: Only the first has the angle not between the two given sides.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Leave every arc and construction line on the page.
- SSS: base, two arcs. SAS: base, angle, measure along. ASA: base, two angles.
- Two angles and a side not between them: find the third angle first.
- Two shorter sides must add to more than the longest.
- SSA can give two triangles.

visuals.alt: Completed SSS construction with all arcs shown, 7, 5 and 6 centimetres

questions.prompt: A triangle is to be constructed from three given side lengths. Which piece of equipment is essential?
questions.solution: Three sides means SSS: the two unknown vertices are found where compass arcs cross. No angles are given, so no protractor is needed.

questions.prompt: Triangle $PQR$ has $PQ = 8$ cm, angle $P = 40°$ and angle $Q = 70°$. Which type of construction is this?
questions.solution: Two angles and the side between them: angle, side, angle.

questions.prompt: Which set of lengths cannot make a triangle?
questions.solution: The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest: $2 + 3 = 5 < 6$, so the arcs never cross.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for constructing triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 7$ cm, $AC = 5$ cm and $BC = 6$ cm in order.
questions.solution: Base first, then one arc from each end, then join. The arcs stay on the page.

markScheme.description: All steps in the correct order

items: Draw $AB$ exactly 7 cm long with a ruler
Set the compasses to 5 cm and draw an arc from $A$
Set the compasses to 6 cm and draw an arc from $B$
Mark $C$ where the arcs cross and join $AC$ and $BC$

questions.prompt: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A = 50°$ and angle $B = 60°$. Work out angle $C$.
questions.solution: Angles in a triangle add to $180°$: $180 - 50 - 60 = 70°$.

questions.prompt: A triangle is constructed with $AB = 6$ cm, angle $A = 35°$ and $AC = 4$ cm. What is drawn at $A$ before the arc?
questions.solution: SAS: the angle at $A$ comes first, then $C$ is marked 4 cm along that line.

markScheme.description: A line at 35° to AB using a protractor

options: A line at $35°$ to $AB$ using a protractor
An arc of radius 4 cm from $B$

questions.prompt: A scale drawing uses 1 cm to represent 2 m. A triangular garden has one side drawn 4.5 cm long. How long is that side in real life, in metres?
Triangle $DEF$ is drawn accurately with $DE = 6$ cm, $DF = 6$ cm and $EF = 6$ cm. Write down the size of angle $D$.
questions.solution: All three sides equal: equilateral, so every angle is $60°$.

questions.prompt: Triangle $ABC$ is constructed with $AB = 10$ cm, $AC = 13$ cm and $BC = 13$ cm. Calculate the perpendicular height from $C$ to $AB$.
questions.solution: The triangle is isosceles, so the perpendicular from $C$ meets $AB$ at its midpoint, 5 cm from $A$. Pythagoras: $h^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, so $h = 12$ cm.

visual.alt: An isosceles triangle with base AB 10 cm and equal sides AC and BC 13 cm

questions.prompt: A student is asked to construct a triangle with $AB = 7$ cm, angle $A = 40°$ and $BC = 5$ cm. Explain why the student could produce two different triangles, and describe how they look.
questions.solution: This is the ambiguous case. It is why SSA is not a condition for congruence, which links to the next topic.

markScheme.description: SSA identified or the arc crossing twice

criteria.text: Recognises the information as two sides and a non-included angle (SSA)
Explains that the arc of radius 5 cm from $B$ crosses the line from $A$ in two places
Describes the two triangles: one with an acute angle at $C$, one with an obtuse angle at $C$, and both satisfy the given information

questions.modelAnswer: The angle at $A$ is not between the two given sides, so this is SSA. Drawing $AB$, then a line from $A$ at $40°$, the compass arc of radius 5 cm centred at $B$ cuts that line twice. Each crossing gives a triangle with $AB = 7$ cm, angle $A = 40°$ and $BC = 5$ cm: one where angle $C$ is acute and $AC$ is longer, one where angle $C$ is obtuse and $AC$ is shorter. The information does not fix the triangle.

questions.prompt: $AB = 7$ cm, angle $A = 40°$ and $BC = 5$ cm, as in the diagram. Take $C$ to be the point where $AC$ is longer. Angle $ACB = 64°$ to the nearest degree. Work out angle $ABC$.
questions.skill: angle sum in the ambiguous case

visual.alt: SSA construction with AB 7 cm, angle A 40 degrees and BC 5 cm, showing the two possible positions of C

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm. Without drawing it, what can you say about its largest angle?
questions.solution: $5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2$, so by the converse of Pythagoras the angle opposite the 13 cm side is a right angle.
options: It cannot be found without drawing

questions.prompt: Triangle $XYZ$ is constructed with $XY = 10$ cm, $XZ = 6$ cm and $YZ = 8$ cm. Calculate its area in cm².
questions.solution: $6^2 + 8^2 = 100 = 10^2$, so the angle at $Z$ is $90°$. Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24$ cm².

markScheme.description: Right angle at $Z$ shown by Pythagoras

questions.prompt: Explain why a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm cannot be constructed, and state the largest whole number of centimetres the 10 cm side could be changed to so that a triangle is possible.
questions.solution: For a triangle, the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side. $4 + 5 = 9$, which is less than 10, so the arcs of radius 4 cm and 5 cm cannot reach each other. The third side must be less than 9 cm, so the largest whole number that works is 8 cm. A common wrong answer is 9 cm, where the arcs only touch and the triangle is flat.

criteria.text: States the triangle inequality: the two shorter sides must add to more than the third
$4 + 5 = 9 < 10$, so the arcs do not meet
Longest side must be less than 9 cm, so 8 cm is the largest whole number that works

questions.modelAnswer: For a triangle, the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side. $4 + 5 = 9$, which is less than 10, so the arcs of radius 4 cm and 5 cm cannot reach each other. The third side must be less than 9 cm; changing 10 cm to 8 cm gives the largest whole-number side that works.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for constructing the perpendicular bisector of a line segment $AB$ in order.
questions.solution: The radius must stay the same for both arcs, and it must be more than half of $AB$ so the arcs meet.

markScheme.description: All steps in the correct order

items: Open the compasses to more than half of $AB$
Draw an arc above and below the line from $A$
Keep the same radius and draw arcs above and below from $B$
Join the two points where the arcs cross

questions.prompt: Explain why every point on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$.
questions.solution: A locus question in disguise: it links constructions to congruence, which is the next topic.

markScheme.description: Equal radii give equidistant crossing points

criteria.text: The construction uses equal radii from $A$ and $B$, so each arc crossing point is equidistant from $A$ and $B$

The line through the two crossing points is the perpendicular bisector, and any point $P$ on it with the midpoint $M$ gives congruent triangles $PMA$ and $PMB$ (SAS: $AM = MB$, right angles at $M$, $PM$ common)
So $PA = PB$ for every point $P$ on the line

questions.modelAnswer: The arcs are drawn with the same radius from $A$ and from $B$, so each crossing point is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$. The line through them passes through the midpoint $M$ of $AB$ at right angles. For any point $P$ on that line, triangles $PMA$ and $PMB$ have $AM = MB$, a right angle at $M$, and $PM$ in common, so they are congruent by SAS and $PA = PB$.

examTechnique.body: Construction questions are 2 or 3 marks and say "use ruler and compasses" or "make an accurate drawing". The marks are for the arcs and the accuracy, within 2 mm and 2°. In this app the drawing itself is done on paper; the questions here test the method, the reasoning, and the calculations examiners attach to a construction.
examinerErrors: Rubbing out construction arcs, which removes the evidence the method mark is based on.
Drawing the arcs freehand or from the wrong end of the base.
Measuring an angle from the wrong scale on the protractor, giving $130°$ instead of $50°$.
Treating SSA as if it fixed one triangle.
Saying a triangle with sides adding exactly to the longest is possible.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the method from the given information, keeps every arc, uses the angle sum to turn a non-included angle into ASA, and can explain the ambiguous case and the triangle inequality in a sentence.
